The Defense Department's authority to provide security assistance and intelligence support, including training, equipment, and logistics, to Ukraine's military and other security forces. Unlike [drawdown](pda-506.qmd) from existing stocks, the initiative buys new equipment from industry, so deliveries take longer but U.S. inventories are not reduced.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: Pub. L. 114-92](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/114/public/92){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Sec. 1250(a): security assistance and intelligence support to Ukraine's military and other security forces.
- Sec. 1250(f): amounts authorized year by year, most recently for fiscal years 2026 and 2027.
- Sec. 1250(h): termination date, now December 31, 2029.
- Sec. 1250(k), added in 2025: equipment bought for Ukraine may be taken into U.S. stocks only in listed circumstances, and must then be replaced for Ukraine.

## Why it matters

The initiative is the Title 10, appropriations-funded path for aiding Ukraine, in contrast to [presidential drawdown](pda-506.qmd) under Title 22. It has been extended and reshaped in nearly every [NDAA](ndaa-annual.qmd) since 2015, which makes it a standing vehicle for congressional direction on Ukraine policy.

## Current status

In force through December 31, 2029, after Sec. 1243 of the FY2026 NDAA (Pub. L. 119-60) extended it and authorized amounts for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Check current status.

[Last checked November 24, 2026.]{.checked}

## Funding and administration

- **Account.** Amounts appropriated to the Defense Department for the initiative.
- **Run by.** The Defense Department.
- **Committees.** Authorizing, House and Senate Armed Services; appropriations, the House and Senate Defense subcommittees.
- **Note.** Funds have come through Defense appropriations acts and Ukraine supplemental appropriations; the FY2026 Defense appropriations act does not name the initiative.
